narrative.what_i_did:
Cut the JoinOrgModal vouch-cosignature collection sub-flow the prior carpenter had named as chip-worthy. Opened with the operator's directive 'Fire up and cut a chunk of the map,' ran the four gates to confirm the cockpit was honest-green from the prior session's hand-off, then surfaced a chip naming the three Phase E4 follow-up threads the prior carpenter had teed up — JoinOrgModal vouch-cosign sub-flow recommended as the most chunk-shaped of the three because it has a clear start and clear end and the picker shape genuinely differs from the existing org-action-context variant. Operator picked the recommended option on one tap. The grounding gate then read the actual code rather than working from the hand-off's sketch: CosignRequestModal.tsx (305 lines) carries an org_action-shaped orgContext prop that funnels through findAuthRule plus isOrgActionRule plus a useMemo that builds an eligible-display list scoped to the rule's eligible set, and renders either a constrained eligible-list picker or the general PeerPicker depending on whether the narrow succeeded; JoinOrgModal.tsx (579 lines) walks the joiner through find then review then optionally proof then send then done, but the requires_vouch send-step just dropped the operator out of the flow with a yellow notice saying 'go collect cosignatures somewhere else, then come back.' The chunk to cut was wiring those two modals together so the joiner has a real button to press instead of a notice telling them to figure it out themselves.

The shape decision was discriminated union versus a sibling prop. The existing orgContext had exactly one caller — MembershipModal.tsx passing orgContext for the threshold-greater-than-one routine-issuance flow — so a discriminated union with kind 'org_action' versus kind 'org_vouch' was a one-line caller update rather than a breaking change with churn. Went with the union because it keeps the surface to one prop name and lets TypeScript's exhaustiveness checker enforce that future kinds get handled everywhere they need to be. The org_vouch variant carries orgName plus threshold and deliberately does NOT carry the orgSelfDecl, because the modal does not need to look up an auth rule in the vouch case — the joiner does not know which of their peers are members of the target org, so the picker is the general PeerPicker over the joiner's full handshake roster rather than a constrained list. The eligible set is open-ended; the org's receive-side gate does the actual vouch-eligibility verification at acceptance time using the evaluateJoinPolicy requires_vouch path that Phase E4 cut 2 shipped. That's the picker-shape difference the prior carpenter named: org_action gates the picker to the rule's eligible set because the rule is the source of truth; org_vouch leaves the picker wide open because the source of truth lives on the org's side, not the joiner's.

A second small change was structurally necessary for the vouch path to work at all: the existing modal lets the operator send exactly once per modal lifecycle. After sent flips true the button disables and the only way to send to another peer is to close and reopen the modal, which loses the signed envelope state. For vouch collection that's broken by construction — the joiner needs to fan their signed self-membership envelope out to several peers (typically two or three depending on the policy's from_any_member_count). Fixed with a useEffect watching recipientTrim that resets sent, sendStatus, and sendError whenever the recipient changes. That also self-corrects misclicks in the org_action constrained-list case, so the change pays for itself on both paths. The banner copy for the vouch variant explicitly tells the operator that the recipient field clears between sends so the fan-out behavior is discoverable from the UI itself rather than buried in the implementation.

The JoinOrgModal wiring side was straightforward: lazy-load CosignRequestModal with the same import pattern MembershipModal and PromoteRouter already use (so the cosign body chunk is not pulled into the JoinOrgModal entry chunk for joiners on non-vouch policies), add a cosignOpen state, and on the send step when policy.kind is requires_vouch render an actionable 'Collect vouch cosignatures' button below the existing amber notice. Tightened the notice copy to point at the button. Mount the lazy CosignRequestModal at the JoinOrgModal root with orgContext of kind org_vouch passing readOrganizationName(orgDecl) and the from_any_member_count threshold. The cosigning manifest's notes paragraph picked up a paragraph naming the new variant and the rationale for the picker-shape divergence. Four gates all pass: typecheck silent, lint silent, 255 of 255 tests in 9.19 seconds, build clean with bundle budgets all in range. JoinOrgModal grew from 579 to 617 lines (still well under the 800-line hard limit), CosignRequestModal grew from 305 to about 340 lines, and the lazy-chunk graph adds no new entry — the cosigning helpers chunk that already serves MembershipModal and PromoteRouter now serves JoinOrgModal too.
narrative.whats_pending:
The vouch sub-flow is structurally complete on the joiner side but the loop-back is not yet wired: when a vouching peer cosigns the self-membership envelope and sends it back via Mycelium, the joiner's wallet needs to absorb the returned cosigned envelope by merging signatures into the locally-held self-membership and then optionally re-fire the cosign collection modal with the new envelope so the joiner can collect the next vouch. The existing AbsorbCosignModal at src/features/cosigning/AbsorbCosignModal.tsx already handles signature-merge for org-issued credentials via mergeSignatures, and the inbox routing layer in envelopeRoute.ts already dispatches incoming envelopes to the right modal — but a returned vouch-cosigned self-membership might land in a slightly different routing slot than a returned org-action cosign. A future cut should walk the routeInbox path in HomeScreen.tsx end-to-end with a vouch-cosigned self-membership envelope to confirm the absorb path lands in the right modal. Also pending: a 'how many vouches do I have so far' surface on JoinOrgModal that reads selfMembership.signatures.length minus one (for the joiner's own signature) and renders progress against the policy threshold. That's a UI niceness, not a correctness gap, but it's the natural next polish.

Beyond the vouch loop, the two remaining appcommander/ metadata files (DOCTRINE_MANIFEST.json and cockpit-cards.json) are still candidates for a folder-closing cleanup sweep — the question remains structurally external to this repo because removing them requires confirming whether the AppCommander cockpit polls them from origin/main, which is a surface the carpenter cannot see from inside this repo. The chip for that decision was named in the prior hand-off and stays available; I deliberately did not surface it this session because the operator's directive named map-chunk feature work specifically.

The two other Phase E4 follow-up threads from the prior carpenter's hand-off are still available: the Phase D charter-amendment chain (new helpers in src/features/governance/ or src/features/connections/, brief should land in project-memory/foreman-memory/projects/tapit-wallet/briefs/ under a charter-amendment-chain-roadmap name) is the multi-session thread; the receiveSelfMembership orgSelfDecl-lookup centralization (small consistency cut to the create-attestation function family) is the tiny one that ships in one session. HomeScreen.tsx ticked from 797 to 798 lines this session (one line of natural drift from unrelated code paths, not from this cut — the build report shows JoinOrgModal at 617 and HomeScreen at 798), still two under the 800-line hard limit, so any feature work that touches HomeScreen will still need an extraction planned in the same commit. The natural extraction candidates remain the inbox-routing dispatcher or one of the four tab-content renderers.
narrative.what_you_could_do_better:
Two honest observations. First, the discriminated-union prop shape choice (kind 'org_action' versus kind 'org_vouch') is the right structural call for keeping the surface narrow and letting TypeScript enforce exhaustiveness, but it creates a coupling between the org_vouch variant's banner copy and the operator's mental model of the requires_vouch policy that is not directly verified anywhere — there is no test (because the codebase pattern is pure-logic tests, not component-render tests) that asserts the banner names the right org or the right threshold, so the only verification path is operator-side. That's the existing project pattern and not a regression, but it means if a future caller passes the wrong orgName or threshold, the modal will display wrong text and nothing catches it before the operator does. A pure-helper extraction (something like buildVouchBannerText(orgName, threshold) returning a structured object the modal renders) would be unit-testable without pulling in jsdom + a component-render harness. Not worth doing now because the function is two strings and a template literal, but worth naming as a pattern if the org-context variants grow further.

Second observation: the useEffect that resets sent/sendStatus/sendError when recipientTrim changes is correct but it fires on EVERY keystroke in the recipient input, which means if the operator types a 64-character pubkey one character at a time, the effect runs 64 times. The effect is cheap (three setState calls), but it also means the banner-status flicker between recipient edits is visually present even when the operator is mid-typing a single recipient. A debounce would be cleaner but is probably over-engineering for this surface. If a future session sees the recipient flicker as actually distracting in operator testing, the fix is either to debounce or to gate the reset on a 'recipient actually changed since the last successful send' boolean rather than 'recipient string mutated.' Worth flagging because the operator is the one who will discover this if it bites, and the carpenter cannot operator-test in the same session that ships the change.
narrative.bigger_picture:
JoinOrgModal is the joiner-side surface of the Phase E4 hybrid-substrate open-joining work that's been ladder-climbing across the last several sessions. The substrate beneath it locked in Phase E4 cut 2: the on-wire envelope shape for a self-membership carries handshake_proof and credential_proof as top-level claim-tree leaves, vouch cosignatures ride envelope.signatures[], and the joiner's own signature covers the proof leaf so it cannot be detached and swapped. Phase E4 cut 3 wired the UI for the four non-vouch policies (open, allow_list, deny_list, requires_handshake, requires_credential) end-to-end. The vouch policy is the one that needed something the other policies don't — a second loop where the joiner reaches out to OTHER wallets, collects their signatures, and only then sends the cosigned envelope to the org. The other policies are single-shot: joiner signs, joiner sends, org accepts or rejects. Vouch is N-to-one: joiner signs, joiner sends to N peers, each peer cosigns and sends back, joiner absorbs each return, joiner sends the cosigned envelope to the org. That N-to-one loop is structurally cosigning, which is why the prior carpenter saw the JoinOrgModal vouch path as fundamentally a cosign-collection problem and named CosignRequestModal as the surface to extend.

The deeper thesis here is that the Tapit Wallet's Layer 2 inter-app signing pathway and the Layer 4 frictionless surface meet at exactly these multi-party flows. A wallet that holds keys and signs is Layer 1; a wallet that lets ANOTHER party request a signature and route the response is Layer 2; a wallet that does both seamlessly through a single coherent UI that the operator does not have to think about is Layer 4. The vouch collection flow is a Layer 4 surface ON a Layer 2 mechanism (multi-party signing) ON Layer 1 keys. Every cut that lets a multi-party flow be expressed as one operator-visible journey rather than 'go do this thing in three different surfaces and bring the results back' is a brick in the Layer 4 wall. This cut adds one brick: the joiner does not have to think 'I need to take my signed envelope somewhere else, find some peers, ask them to cosign through a different flow, absorb each response, then reopen JoinOrgModal' — they tap one button and the cosign collection happens inside the same modal stack they started in.

The pattern of reusing CosignRequestModal as the substrate for both org_action (signer-side, constrained-eligible) AND org_vouch (joiner-side, open-eligible) collection is also worth naming. Both flows are 'fan a signed envelope out to N peers and absorb each return' — the only structural difference is whether the eligible set is closed or open. By making that difference a discriminated-union prop rather than two sibling modals, the cosigning feature now has a clean place to add a third variant in the future if some policy kind comes along that needs yet another picker shape (e.g. 'eligible peers are those who hold a specific credential' — that's a closed set derivable at picker time but neither pre-named in a rule nor open to all peers; it would be its own kind). The substrate is now generic enough to absorb that without a structural rewrite — the kind discriminant absorbs the variation.

The two-commit comms-v2 arc that the prior two sessions delivered (hygiene cut plus appcommander/ targeted sweep) is what made THIS session feel small and clean. Fire up, ground, surface chip, cut, gates, write narrative, fire down. Each removal in that arc is paid back here in this session's wake-up time. The reinforcing loop is doing what it was designed to do — the next carpenter will read this narrative, see the vouch sub-flow shipped, and either polish the loop-back or pivot to the next Phase E4 thread without having to reconstruct the substrate from scratch.

feedback_to_appcommander: The discriminated-union pattern for the org-context prop is a clean substrate-reuse pattern worth noting in the skeleton. Most carpenter sessions face a 'should I extend the existing modal or build a sibling?' decision when a new flow needs a slightly different shape of the same primitive — the right answer is usually 'extend with a discriminated-union variant prop' when the underlying signing-and-send mechanic is the same, and 'build a sibling' only when the mechanic itself differs. CosignRequestModal now has two variants (org_action signer-side, org_vouch joiner-side) sharing one signing-and-send loop, and the next variant (whatever policy kind comes along that needs a different picker) drops in as a third kind without restructuring. Worth lifting into the AppCommander-side doctrine as a pattern note: 'when extending a modal with a new flow, prefer a discriminated-union variant prop over a sibling modal when the signing-and-send mechanic is shared.'
